name: Independent State of Croatia
info: A Second World War Axis puppet state ruled by Ante Pavelić's fascist Ustaše in occupied Yugoslavia from 1941 to 1945, which carried out a genocide against Serbs, Jews and Roma.

facts.founder: Proclaimed by Slavko Kvaternik for Ante Pavelić, with German and Italian backing
facts.predecessor: Kingdom of Yugoslavia (occupied by the Axis)

t: The Independent State of Croatia was proclaimed in Zagreb on 10 April 1941 after the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia, and the Nuremberg Military Tribunal later concluded it was not a sovereign state.
The Ustaše regime killed an estimated 320,000–340,000 Serbs, 30,000 Croatian Jews and 30,000 Roma; Jasenovac was the largest of its 22 concentration camps.
Partisan resistance began in the NDH in June 1941, and the state ended in May 1945, its territory becoming part of Democratic Federal Yugoslavia.
dyk: The Duke of Aosta, named King Tomislav II of the state, never visited it; on learning of his nomination he thought it a bad joke by his cousin King Victor Emmanuel III.
ev: Slavko Kvaternik proclaims the Independent State of Croatia in Zagreb under German protection
Ante Pavelić returns from exile in Italy and takes power as Poglavnik
The Treaties of Rome cede central Dalmatia, most Adriatic islands and other lands to Italy
The Sisak Partisan Detachment, celebrated as the first armed resistance unit in occupied Yugoslavia, is formed
The first formal agreement between Bosnian Chetniks and the Ustaše authorities is concluded
After Italy's armistice the NDH declares the Treaties of Rome void and annexes the Dalmatian lands ceded to Italy
The Lorković-Vokić coup against Pavelić fails and its conspirators are executed
NDH forces and civilians retreat to Austria; the British hand them to the Partisans, and the state falls after the Battle of Odžak on 25 May

sections.foundation:
The Ustaše grew out of Croatian resentment of the centralised Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, proclaimed in 1918. After the Croatian Peasant Party leader Stjepan Radić was shot in the Belgrade parliament in 1928, King Alexander proclaimed a royal dictatorship in January 1929, and the Ustaša was created in principle that year. Ante Pavelić, a former Zagreb deputy, went into exile in Italy, where Benito Mussolini gave the Ustaše training grounds in exchange for Pavelić's agreement that Dalmatia would go to Italy.

The Axis powers invaded and occupied Yugoslavia in 1941. Vladko Maček, leader of the Croatian Peasant Party, refused their offer to form a government. On 10 April 1941, with the German army in control of Zagreb, the retired lieutenant-colonel Slavko Kvaternik proclaimed the Independent State of Croatia in the name of Pavelić. Pavelić returned on 15 April and took power the next day as Poglavnik and prime minister. The Ustaše had fewer than 12,000 members when the war started. Under Italian pressure Pavelić accepted Aimone, Duke of Aosta, as a figurehead king, Tomislav II.
sections.socioeconomy:
The economy was subordinated to Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. A May 1941 agreement gave Germany unrestricted access to industrial raw materials and made the NDH pay for German troops on its soil; Italy's short-term agreements required supplies, monthly payments and free logging. Both demanded bauxite, iron ore, wood and grain. The Germans took the Ljubija iron mines, the Sarajevo–Tuzla–Zenica industrial complex and the bauxite, and about 200,000 citizens of the NDH were sent to Germany as slave and forced labourers. In 1942, 80% of exports went to Germany and 12% to Italy.

Businesses owned by Jews and Serbs were placed under state commissars, and on 10 December 1941 the postal bank accounts of Serbs, Jews and Roma were confiscated. The currency, the kuna, was printed to pay for the upkeep of foreign troops, and circulation rose thirty-two-fold between April 1941 and May 1945. The German Foreign Ministry put the population at about 6,285,000, of whom 52.5% were Croats and 30.6% Serbs. The Croatian University in Zagreb was the only university, and four state theatres played in Zagreb, Osijek, Dubrovnik and Sarajevo.
sections.military:
The Army of the Independent State of Croatia, the Home Guard, was founded in April 1941 with the Wehrmacht's consent, beside the Ustaše Militia and a gendarmerie. First limited to 16,000 men, it grew to about 55,000 by mid-1941 and to 130,000 in early 1943. Under the Treaties of Rome its navy was kept to a few coastal and patrol craft. The air force began with captured Yugoslav aircraft, and its Croatian Air Force Legion fought beside the Luftwaffe on the Eastern Front from 1941 to 1943.

The Partisans led by Josip Broz Tito, joined by Croats, Serbs, Bosniaks and others, soon controlled much of the NDH, leaving garrison towns in a de facto state of siege; in 1944 Croats formed 61% of the Partisan units from the Federal State of Croatia. Conscripts' morale fell, many defected or passed supplies to the Partisans, and the army shrank to 70,000 by late 1944. From 1942 the Ustaše made agreements with Bosnian Chetniks to fight the Partisans together. In May 1945 about 120,000 NDH troops were handed to the Partisans by the British, and about half were killed in the Bleiburg repatriations.
sections.governance:
The NDH was a one-party state: every party but the Ustaše was banned, and Ante Pavelić ruled absolutely as Poglavnik. It was formally a monarchy from the Laws of the Crown of Zvonimir of 15 May 1941, but Tomislav II never visited it and abdicated on 31 July 1943. Pavelić then became head of state and in September 1943 appointed Nikola Mandić prime minister. A parliament created by decree on 24 January 1942 was not elected and could not legislate; it met just over a dozen times. The Ustaše Surveillance Service, set up in August 1941, suppressed opposition, and Maček was interned in the Jasenovac concentration camp.

The state was divided into 22 great parishes under Grand Župans, with districts, cities and municipalities, and kept Yugoslavia's courts under their older names. From 1941 to 1943 it was split into German and Italian zones. Its laws from April 1941 made any offence to the Croatian nation treason punishable by death and introduced racial laws modelled on Nazi Germany. The minister Milovan Žanić declared in May 1941 that the country must be cleansed of Serbs. The Axis powers and Spain recognised it.
sections.impact:
The NDH covered most of present-day Croatia, all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, part of Serbia and a small part of Slovenia, while Italy and Hungary took Dalmatia, the islands, Međimurje and southern Baranja. Its main effect on the people within it was genocide. The regime killed an estimated 320,000–340,000 Serbs, 30,000 Croatian Jews and 30,000 Roma, including between 77,000 and 99,000 people killed at Jasenovac, and forced about 300,000 Serbs out. Jastrebarsko and Sisak held only children. Jonathan Steinberg called the crimes against Serbs the earliest total genocide attempted during the Second World War. From May 1943 Croatian Jews were deported by cattle car to Auschwitz.

The Ustaše also killed and imprisoned Croats who opposed them; Ivo Goldstein estimates 135,000 Croats died in the NDH, among them Partisans, the regime's opponents and suspected collaborators killed by the Partisans. A German Gestapo report of February 1942 blamed the growth of resistance chiefly on Ustaše atrocities against the Orthodox population. The resistance in the NDH and Bosnia made up most of the Partisan movement's strength.
sections.decline:
Hitler grew angry that Pavelić's policies inflamed rebellion and tied down German troops, and in 1942 he summoned Pavelić to Vinnytsia; Slavko Kvaternik was replaced and sent into exile. When Italy capitulated in September 1943, the Italian zone was abolished and the German zone covered the whole state, which annexed the Dalmatian lands ceded in 1941, though much of them was held by the Partisans. In August 1944 Mladen Lorković and Ante Vokić tried a coup to change sides to the Allies; it failed and they were executed.

By early 1945 the army withdrew towards Zagreb with German and Cossack troops, and the advance of the Partisans and the Soviet Red Army drove a mass retreat towards Austria. Pavelić fled, and on 6 May 1945 the regime emptied the bank vaults of the state's gold. The British refused the retreating columns entry into Austria and turned them over to the Partisans; the Bleiburg repatriations ended in mass executions. On 25 May 1945 the Battle of Odžak ended the state, and its territory became part of Democratic Federal Yugoslavia. Pavelić died in Spain in 1959; other ministers were tried with Mile Budak.

summary: The Independent State of Croatia was an Axis puppet state set up in occupied Yugoslavia in April 1941 and ruled by Ante Pavelić's Ustaše as a one-party fascist state. It carried out a genocide against Serbs, Jews and Roma, served German and Italian economic demands, and collapsed before the Partisans in May 1945.
references: Tomasevich, Jozo, War and Revolution in Yugoslavia: 1941–1945

pointDescs.1941: The NDH is proclaimed on 10 April and its army grows to about 55,000 men by mid-year, while Partisan resistance begins.
pointDescs.1942: The army reaches its largest size, 130,000 by early 1943, and agreements with Bosnian Chetniks are signed against the Partisans.
pointDescs.1943: Italy capitulates; the NDH annexes Dalmatia on paper but the Partisans hold much of it.
pointDescs.1944: The Lorković-Vokić coup fails and the army shrinks to 70,000 by late in the year.
pointDescs.1945: The state collapses in May; the Battle of Odžak on 25 May is its end.

notes: Only five points: the state lasted four years; the brief asks 8-20 with years, and the article's events fall in 1941-1945 only, so one point per year was used. The editor may wish to allow this or use fractional years.
The article has no source list; Tomasevich's book is cited by name in the text, without publisher or year, and is the only reference.
Tags are a poor fit: no 'Fascist' or 'Puppet' tag exists in the list; 'Colonial' stands for a state under foreign occupation. The editor may prefer others.

Population and casualty figures are as the article gives them; deportation figures conflict within the article (120,000 deported and 300,000 fled by 1943 vs about 300,000 deported or fled by the war's end); the text says 'forced about 300,000 Serbs out', following the genocide section.
